section.heading: 5.4 Eigenvectors and Linear Transformations
section.paragraph: In this section, we will look at eigenvalues and eigenvectors of linear transformations $$T:V\rightarrow V$$ , where $$V$$ is any vector space. In the case where $$V$$ is a finite dimensional vector space and there is a basis for $$V$$ consisting of eigenvectors of $$T$$ , we will see how to represent the transformation $$T$$ as left multiplication by a diagonal matrix.
section.heading: Eigenvectors of Linear Transformations
section.paragraph: Previously, we looked at a variety of vector spaces including the discrete-time signal space, $$\mathbb{S}$$ , and the set of polynomials, $$\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}$$ . Eigenvalues and eigenvectors can be defined for linear transformations from any vector space to itself.

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: Let $$V$$ be a vector space. An eigenvector of a linear transformation $$T:V\rightarrow V$$ is a nonzero vector $$\textbf{x}$$ in $$V$$ such that $$T(\textbf{x}) = \text{λ} \textbf{x}$$ for some scalar $$\text{λ}$$ . A scalar $$\text{λ}$$ is called an eigenvalue of $$T$$ if there is a nontrivial solution $$\textbf{x}$$ of $$T(\textbf{x}) = \text{λ} \textbf{x}$$ ; such an $$\textbf{x}$$ is called an eigenvector corresponding to $$\text{λ}$$ .

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: The sinusoidal signals were studied in detail in Sections 4.7 and 4.8. Consider the signal defined by $$\text{\{} s_{k} \text{\}} = \left\{ {\cos\left( \frac{k\pi}{2} \right)} \right\}$$ , where $$k$$ ranges over all integers. The left double-shift linear transformation $$D$$ is defined by $$D(\{ x_{k}\}) = \{ x_{k + 2}\}$$ . Show that $$\{ s_{k}\}$$ is an eigenvector of $$D$$ and determine the associated eigenvalue.
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: The trigonometric formula $$\cos(\theta + \pi) = - \cos(\theta)$$ is useful here. Set $$\{ y_{k}\} = D(\{ s_{k}\})$$ and observe that
$$y_{k} = s_{k + 2} = cos \left(\frac{\left(\right. k + 2 \left.\right) \pi}{2}\right) = cos \left(\frac{k \pi}{2} + \pi\right) = - cos \left(\frac{k \pi}{2}\right) = - s_{k}$$
and so $$D(\{ s_{k}\}) = \{ - s_{k}\} = - \{ s_{k}\}$$ . This establishes that $$\{ s_{k}\}$$ is an eigenvector of $$D$$ with eigenvalue $$- 1$$ .

section.heading: The Matrix of a Linear Transformation
section.paragraph: There are branches of linear algebra that use infinite dimensional matrices to transform infinite dimensional vector spaces; however, in the remainder of this chapter we will restrict our study to linear transformations and matrices associated with finite dimensional vector spaces.

Let $$V$$ be an $$n \text{-dimensional}$$ vector space and let $$T$$ be any linear transformation from $$V$$ to $$V$$ . To associate a matrix with $$T$$ , choose any basis $$B$$ for $$V$$ . Given any $$\textbf{x}$$ in $$V$$ , the coordinate vector $$\lbrack\textbf{x}\rbrack_{B}$$ is in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ , as is the coordinate vector of its image, $$\lbrack T(\textbf{x})\rbrack_{B}$$ .

The connection between $$\lbrack\textbf{x}\rbrack_{B}$$ and $$\lbrack T(\textbf{x})\rbrack_{B}$$ is easy to find. Let $$\{\textbf{b}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{b}_{n}\}$$ be the basis $$B$$ for $$V$$ . If $$\textbf{x} = r_{1}\textbf{b}_{1} + \cdots + r_{n}\textbf{b}_{n}$$ , then
$$\left([ \textbf{x} ]\right)_{B} = \begin{bmatrix} r_{1} \\ \vdots \\ r_{n} \end{bmatrix}$$
and

$$T \left(\right. \textbf{x} \left.\right) = T \left(\right. r_{1} \textbf{b}_{1} + \hdots + r_{n} \textbf{b}_{n} \left.\right) = r_{1} T \left(\right. \textbf{b}_{1} \left.\right) + \hdots + r_{n} T \left(\right. \textbf{b}_{n} \left.\right)$$
because $$T$$ is linear. Now, since the coordinate mapping from $$V$$ to $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ is linear (Theorem 8 in Section 4.4), equation (1) leads to

$$\left[\right. T \left(\right. \textbf{x} \left.\right) \left]\right._{B} = r_{1} \left[\right. T \left(\right. \textbf{b}_{1} \left.\right) \left]\right._{B} + \hdots + r_{n} \left[\right. T \left(\right. \textbf{b}_{n} \left.\right) \left]\right._{B}$$
Since $$B \text{-coordinate}$$ vectors are in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ , the vector equation (2) can be written as a matrix equation, namely
$$\boxed{\left[\right. T \left(\right. \textbf{x} \left.\right) \left]\right._{B} = M \left[\right. \textbf{x} \left]\right._{B}}$$
where

$$\boxed{M = \left[\right. \left[\right. T \left(\right. \textbf{b}_{1} \left.\right) \left]\right._{B} \left[\right. T \left(\right. \textbf{b}_{2} \left.\right) \left]\right._{B} \hdots \left[\right. T \left(\right. \textbf{b}_{n} \left.\right) \left]\right._{B} \left]\right.}$$
The matrix $$M$$ is a matrix representation of $$T$$ , called the matrix for T relative to basis $$B$$ (or $$B$$ -matrix) and denoted by $$\lbrack T\rbrack_{B}$$ . See Figure 2.

image.alt: A figure shows two ways of linearly transforming a vector.

section.paragraph: Equation (3) says that, so far as coordinate vectors are concerned, the action of $$T$$ on $$\textbf{x}$$ may be viewed as left-multiplication by $$M$$ .

section.heading: Linear Transformations on ℝn
section.paragraph: In an applied problem involving $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ , a linear transformation $$T$$ usually appears first as a matrix transformation, $$\textbf{x}\mapsto A\textbf{x}$$ . If $$A$$ is diagonalizable, then there is a basis $$B$$ for $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ consisting of eigenvectors of $$A$$ . Theorem 8 below shows that, in this case, the $$B \text{-matrix}$$ for $$T$$ is diagonal. Diagonalizing $$A$$ amounts to finding a diagonal matrix representation of $$\textbf{x}\mapsto A\textbf{x}$$ .

note.title: Theorem ﻿8﻿
note.heading: Theorem ﻿8﻿
Diagonal Matrix Representation
note.paragraph: Suppose $$A = PDP^{- 1}$$ , where $$D$$ is a diagonal $$n \times n$$ matrix. If $$B$$ is the basis for $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ formed from the columns of $$P$$ , then $$D$$ is the $$B \text{-matrix}$$ for the transformation $$\textbf{x}\mapsto A\textbf{x}$$ .

section.heading: Proof﻿
section.paragraph: Denote the columns of $$P$$ by $$\textbf{b}_{1},\ldots \text{,} \textbf{b}_{n}$$ , so that $$B = \{\textbf{b}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{b}_{n}\}$$ and $$P = \left\lbrack {\textbf{b}_{1}\cdots\textbf{b}_{n}} \right\rbrack$$ . In this case, $$P$$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix $$P_{B}$$ discussed in Section 4.4, where
$$P \left(\left[\right. \mathbf{x} \left]\right.\right)_{\mathbf{\mathit{B}}} = \mathbf{x} \text{and} \left(\left[\right. \mathbf{x} \left]\right.\right)_{B} = P^{- 1} \mathbf{x}$$
If $$T(\textbf{x}) = A\textbf{x}$$ for $$\textbf{x}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ , then

$$\left(\left[\right. T \left]\right.\right)_{B} & = & \left[\right. \left(\left[\right. T \left(\right. \mathbf{b}_{1} \left.\right) \left]\right.\right)_{B} \hdots \left(\left[\right. T \left(\right. \mathbf{b}_{n} \left.\right) \left]\right.\right)_{B} \left]\right. & \text{Definition} \text{of} \left(\left[\right. T \left]\right.\right)_{B} & = & \left[\right. \left(\left[\right. A \mathbf{b}_{1} \left]\right.\right)_{B} \hdots \left(\left[\right. A \mathbf{b}_{n} \left]\right.\right)_{B} \left]\right. & \text{Since} T \left(\mathbf{x}\right) = A \mathbf{x} & = & \left[\right. P^{- 1} A \mathbf{b}_{1} \hdots P^{- 1} A \mathbf{b}_{n} \left]\right. & \text{Change} \text{of} \text{coordinates} & = & P^{- 1} A \left[\right. \mathbf{b}_{1} \hdots \mathbf{b}_{n} \left]\right. & \text{Matrix} \text{multiplication} & = & P^{- 1} A P &$$
Since $$A = PDP^{- 1}$$ , we have $$\left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} T \end{array} \right\rbrack_{B} = P^{- 1}AP = D$$ .

Find a basis $$B$$ for $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ with the property that the $$B \text{-matrix}$$ for $$T$$ is a diagonal matrix.

The columns of $$P$$ , call them $$\textbf{b}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{b}_{2}$$ , are eigenvectors of $$A$$ . By Theorem 8, $$D$$ is the $$B \text{-matrix}$$ for $$T$$ when $$B = \{\textbf{b}_{1},\textbf{b}_{2}\}$$ . section.heading: Similarity of Matrix Representations
section.paragraph: The proof of Theorem 8 did not use the information that $$D$$ was diagonal. Hence, if $$A$$ is similar to a matrix $$C$$ , with $$A = PCP^{- 1}$$ , then $$C$$ is the $$B \text{-matrix}$$ for the transformation $$\textbf{x}\mapsto A\textbf{x}$$ when the basis $$B$$ is formed from the columns of $$P$$ . The factorization $$A = PCP^{- 1}$$ is shown in Figure 4.

image.alt: A figure shows four arrows forming a rectangle with matrix notations on its vertices.

figure.caption: Figure 4 Similarity of two matrix representations: A = PCP-1

section.paragraph: Conversely, if $$T:\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ is defined by $$T(\textbf{x}) = A\textbf{x}$$ , and if $$B$$ is any basis for $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ , then the $$B \text{-matrix}$$ for $$T$$ is similar to $$A$$ . In fact, the calculations in the proof of Theorem 8 show that if $$P$$ is the matrix whose columns come from the vectors in $$B$$ , then $$\lbrack T\rbrack_{B} = P^{- 1}AP$$ . This important connection between the matrix of a linear transformation and similar matrices is highlighted here.

note.paragraph: The set of all matrices similar to a matrix $$A$$ coincides with the set of all matrix representations of the transformation $$\textbf{x}\mapsto A\textbf{x}$$ .

example.heading: Example 5
example.paragraph: Let $$A = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} 4 & {- 9} \\ 4 & {- 8} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\textbf{b}_{1} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 3 \\ 2 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , and $$\textbf{b}_{2} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 2 \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . The characteristic polynomial of $$A$$ is $$( \text{λ} + 2)^{2}$$ , but the eigenspace for the eigenvalue $$- 2$$ is only one-dimensional; so $$A$$ is not diagonalizable. However, the basis $$B = \{\textbf{b}_{1},\textbf{b}_{2}\}$$ has the property that the $$B \text{-matrix}$$ for the transformation $$\textbf{x}\mapsto A\textbf{x}$$ is a triangular matrix called the Jordan form of $$A$$ .1 Find this $$B \text{-matrix}$$ .
